analysis.investment_thesis: UTLSOLAR fails both legs of the Magic Formula spectacularly — earnings yield of ~2.8% (EBIT ₹235 Cr / EV ~₹8,321 Cr) is far below the 12% minimum, and ROCE of 16.6% is below the 20% threshold for a "good" business. At a P/E of 402x, the market has priced in decades of flawless execution, leaving no margin of safety.
key_strengths: Revenue growing at 38.8% CAGR (5Y) with operating income accelerating even faster at 53.1% CAGR — real business momentum
Solar/EV charging exposure in a structurally growing Indian market with government tailwinds
Operating margin expanded sharply to 17.2% in FY25 (from ~9% in FY20), suggesting some operating leverage
key_risks: Earnings quality is deeply suspect: FY25 net profit ₹156 Cr but OCF only ₹18 Cr and FCF -₹101 Cr — massive working capital drain or receivables buildup
Valuation is near-delusional at P/E 402x and EV/EBITDA ~20x; earnings yield of 2.8% offers no cushion against any earnings disappointment
Debt nearly doubled YoY (₹205 Cr → ₹395 Cr) while finance costs compound at 61.6% CAGR, eroding the ROE quality (D/E 1.38)
red_flags: FCF deeply negative (-₹101 Cr) in FY25 despite ₹156 Cr reported net profit — 87% earnings-to-cash conversion gap is a serious red flag
Promoter holding at 86.76% severely limits free float and raises governance concentration risk
OCF positive in only 3 of last 5 years — business consistently consumes more cash than it generates operationally
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Using Greenblatt's Magic Formula, UTLSOLAR scores poorly on both critical dimensions. Earnings Yield (EBIT/EV) = ₹235 Cr / ₹8,321 Cr ≈ 2.8% — that's roughly one-fifth of the 12% minimum I require, meaning you're paying a massive premium relative to what the business earns. Return on Capital (proxied by ROCE) at 16.6% is below the 20% threshold for a genuinely "good" business, and ROE of 58% is artificially inflated by 1.38x D/E leverage. Neither metric qualifies; both together make this a clear avoid under any systematic value screen.

The FY25 financials reveal a deeper problem: while the income statement shows a stunning ₹156 Cr net profit, operating cash flow was only ₹18 Cr and free cash flow was -₹101 Cr. This gap — roughly ₹138 Cr between reported profit and operating cash — suggests aggressive revenue recognition, surging receivables, or working capital tied up in solar project execution. Capex of ₹119 Cr on top compounds the cash burn. The business may be real and growing, but at P/E 402x the stock prices in perfection while delivering mediocre FCF. This is precisely the type of high-P/E, low-earnings-yield, capital-hungry business the Magic Formula is designed to avoid.
